processing: Little is recorded for this name; a fully oxidised black tea, and the 'golden needle' name points to a bud-rich pick, as with other needle-style blacks.
harvest_season: Not specifically recorded; bud-rich black teas are typically spring pickings.
appearance_dry: As the name suggests, slender needles with golden down.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden red, as is usual for bud-heavy Fujian black tea.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting record exists for this name; bud-heavy Fujian blacks are typically honeyed and smooth, with little bitterness.

brewing.notes: General advice for bud-heavy black tea: cooler water and short steeps.

vintage_note: Nothing specific is recorded for this name. Black teas of this kind are usually sold as a recent spring harvest, with the budded grades priced highest; ask for the year, and drink within a couple of years.
description:
Bai Lin Jin Zhen, 'Bailin golden needle', appears on Chinese black tea lists under the name of Bailin, a town in Fuding in northeast Fujian. Little else is on record, so it is best understood as a needle-style relative of the area's better-known Bailin Gongfu.

Bailin Gongfu is one of the three Min Hong black teas of Fujian, alongside Zhenghe and Tanyang. Fuding is better known abroad for white tea, and the Fuding Da Bai bush commonly used for its silver needle is also said to be the usual raw material for Bailin black. Whether this needle tea uses it is not recorded.

If you find a lot, brew it as you would any bud-heavy black tea, with cooler water and quick steeps. Ask the seller about the cultivar and the picking, since the name alone guarantees little.
history: Little is documented about this tea by name, and no date or maker can be tied to it. The local black tea tradition around Bailin is better recorded: early in the twentieth century growers there, including the Chen family, are said to have begun making black tea from Fuding Da Bai leaf, and a 2024 group standard now covers Bailin Gongfu.
